hints: Each move turns k piles into 1, so the pile count drops by exactly k−1. When is it even possible to end with a single pile from n piles?

Interval DP. dp[i][j] = min cost to squeeze piles i..j into as few piles as possible. Split at m stepping by k−1 so the left part becomes exactly one pile; whenever the range can become one pile, add its total sand (prefix sums).

1. If (n - 1) % (k - 1) != 0, return -1.
  2. Build prefix sums of the piles.
  3. For length from k to n, for each i (j = i + length - 1):
  4. dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][m] + dp[m+1][j]) for m = i, i+k−1, i+2(k−1), … < j.
  5. If (j - i) % (k - 1) == 0, add sum(i..j) (the final fuse of this range). Return dp[0][n-1].

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every sequence of fuse moves recursively.

approaches.name: 3D DP
approaches.idea: f[i][j][p] = min cost to turn piles i..j into p piles.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: 2D interval DP with split points stepping by k−1.

explain: For [4, 1, 3, 2] with k = 2: fusing 4+1 (cost 5) and 3+2 (cost 5), then 5+5 (cost 10) totals 20, which the DP finds by splitting the whole range in the middle and adding the full sum 10 at the top. With k = 3 the same piles give -1, because 4 piles drop by 2 each move and can never reach exactly 1. Stepping m by k−1 guarantees the left part i..m can be one pile, and the sum is added exactly when the whole range collapses to one pile. A single pile costs 0.
recognize: 'Merge exactly k adjacent groups, cost = their total, minimise to one group' → interval DP with prefix sums and a feasibility check.
